solution.concept_anchor: NHRC statutory basis and Paris Principles accreditation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students conflate 'constitutional' with 'statutory' when they see NHRC described as a high-powered national body, assuming it must have constitutional backing like the Election Commission.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): NHRC has no Article in the Constitution establishing it; it derives from an Act of Parliament, unlike the Election Commission under Article 324.
Eliminate (b): NHRC's parent legislation is the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 — not 1990; the 1990 date is a temporal-swap trap.
Eliminate (d): NHRC's 'A-status' accreditation comes from GANHRI under UN Paris Principles (1991), not from a bilateral treaty with the UN.
Confirm (c): NHRC is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, which also governs SHRCs — the same Act covers both.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is the entity-swap between constitutional and statutory bodies. NHRC handles matters of constitutional rights but is not itself a constitutional body — a distinction UPSC exploits repeatedly. Students who associate 'human rights' with 'constitutional rights' incorrectly infer constitutional status for NHRC.
solution.final_explanation:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 — a parliamentary statute, not a constitutional provision. This distinguishes it from bodies like the Election Commission (Article 324) which have direct constitutional backing.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: NHRC is a statutory body, not a constitutional body. No article of the Constitution establishes it.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The parent Act is from 1993, not 1990. The 1993 Act also governs State Human Rights Commissions.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 is the parent legislation. The same Act provides for both NHRC and SHRCs, though under different provisions.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: NHRC's 'A-status' is granted by GANHRI (Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions) based on compliance with the UN Paris Principles (1991) — not through a UN treaty obligation.

Value Addition:
• The Act has been amended in 2006 and 2019 — the 2019 amendment is the most UPSC-relevant.
• Paris Principles (1991) set global standards for national human rights institutions: independence, broad mandate, and public accessibility.
• SHRC Chairperson is a retired Chief Justice of a High Court; NHRC Chairperson post-2019 can be a retired CJI or retired SC judge.

solution.concept_anchor: Post-2019 NHRC Chairperson eligibility expansion

statement_analysis.statement: Prior to the 2019 amendment, only a retired Chief Justice of India was eligible to be appointed as Chairperson of the NHRC.
statement_analysis.reason: The original Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 restricted the Chairperson's post exclusively to a retired Chief Justice of India — a narrower criterion than what the 2019 amendment introduced.

statement_analysis.statement: Following the 2019 amendment, a retired Judge of any High Court is also eligible to be appointed as Chairperson of the NHRC.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2019 amendment expanded eligibility to include a retired Judge of the Supreme Court (not High Court). A retired High Court judge is eligible only for the Chairperson of a State Human Rights Commission.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairperson of NHRC is appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of a High-Powered Committee.
statement_analysis.reason: The President makes the appointment based on the recommendation of the High-Powered Committee comprising the Prime Minister, Speaker of Lok Sabha, Home Minister, and Leaders of Opposition in both Houses.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is the strongest distractor because both Statements 1 and 3 are individually correct, and students who are confused about Statement 2 (conflating Supreme Court with High Court) may mistakenly include it, leading them to choose 'all three' or a combination including Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Pre-2019, only a retired CJI was eligible — this is well-established and correct.

Reject Statement 2: The 2019 amendment extended eligibility to retired Supreme Court judges, not High Court judges. High Court retired judges head SHRCs, not NHRC — this is a classic geographic/entity-swap trap.
Confirm Statement 3: Presidential appointment on recommendation of the High-Powered Committee is unchanged and correct.
Select option (b): Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits a conflation between NHRC and SHRC appointment criteria. A retired High Court Chief Justice heads a SHRC. After 2019, a retired SC judge (not HC judge) can head NHRC. Students who have memorised 'expansion in 2019' without precision will pick the High Court option, making Statement 2 appear correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2019 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act significantly altered NHRC's composition and eligibility criteria. Understanding the exact scope of that expansion is critical.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Before 2019, the Chairperson post was reserved exclusively for a retired Chief Justice of India, making it one of the most restrictive eligibility criteria among statutory bodies.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 2019 amendment expanded eligibility to a retired Judge of the Supreme Court — not any High Court. A retired Chief Justice of a High Court is the eligibility criterion for SHRC Chairperson, not NHRC. This is the most commonly confused distinction.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The appointment mechanism via the President on recommendation of a High-Powered Committee (headed by PM) remains intact and was not altered by the 2019 amendment.

Value Addition:
• The expansion of NHRC Chairperson eligibility was debated because critics felt it diluted the prestige of the post.
• SHRC Chairperson = retired Chief Justice of a High Court; NHRC Chairperson (post-2019) = retired CJI or retired SC Judge.
• The 2019 amendment also made it mandatory to have at least one woman member on the NHRC.

solution.concept_anchor: High-Powered Committee composition for NHRC appointment

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice President of India) is a member of the High-Powered Committee that recommends appointments to the NHRC.
statement_analysis.reason: It is the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha — not the Chairman (Vice President) — who is a member of the High-Powered Committee. This is a deliberate and frequently exploited distinction.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is a member of the High-Powered Committee for NHRC appointments.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is explicitly named as a member of the High-Powered Committee under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

statement_analysis.statement: The Leaders of Opposition in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha are members of the High-Powered Committee for NHRC appointments.
statement_analysis.reason: Both the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and the Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha are statutory members of the High-Powered Committee, ensuring bipartisan oversight.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who recall that the Vice President is associated with Rajya Sabha and assume the 'Chairman of Rajya Sabha' (i.e., VP) is on the committee, not the Deputy Chairman.
elimination_logic: Identify Statement 1: The Vice President chairs Rajya Sabha but is NOT on the NHRC appointment committee — it is the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha who is a member. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 2: Speaker of Lok Sabha is indeed on the committee — Statement 2 is correct.
Verify Statement 3: Both Leaders of Opposition in both Houses are members — Statement 3 is correct.
Since the question asks which is NOT correct, and only Statement 1 is incorrect, select option (c): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces 'Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha' with 'Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Vice President).' Students who know the Vice President's role as Rajya Sabha Chairman often assume he sits on high-powered committees related to Parliament's functioning. The Act specifically names the Deputy Chairman, not the Chairman, making this a precision-recall trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The High-Powered Committee that recommends NHRC appointments consists of: Prime Minister (Chair), Speaker of Lok Sabha, Union Home Minister, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha, and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Vice President of India, who chairs the Rajya Sabha, is NOT a member of this committee. The Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha is the member — a critical distinction UPSC has exploited.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Speaker of Lok Sabha is a statutory member of the High-Powered Committee.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Both Leaders of Opposition (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) are members, ensuring cross-party representation in appointments.

Value Addition:
• The same committee structure (with minor variations) is used for other appointments — compare with the CBI Director appointment committee which includes the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India.
• This bipartisan structure is intended to prevent purely executive control over human rights oversight.
• The Home Minister's presence on the committee is sometimes cited as a conflict of interest, since the Home Ministry oversees police forces frequently complained against.

solution.concept_anchor: 2019 amendment changes to NHRC composition

statement_analysis.statement: The 2019 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act made it mandatory to include at least one woman member in the NHRC.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2019 amendment explicitly introduced the requirement of at least one woman member, a new affirmative representation provision not present in the original 1993 Act.

statement_analysis.statement: After the 2019 amendment, the NHRC can have up to five full members (excluding ex-officio members).
statement_analysis.reason: The 2019 amendment raised the maximum number of members from four to five, broadening the Commission's deliberative capacity.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairperson of the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) was added as an ex-officio member of NHRC by the 2019 amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2019 amendment added the Chairpersons of NCBC and NCPCR to the list of ex-officio members, expanding the original list which included NCW, NCM, NCSC, and NCST.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2019 amendment extended the tenure of the NHRC Chairperson and members from 3 years to 5 years.
statement_analysis.reason: The tenure remains 3 years or until age 70, whichever is earlier. The 2019 amendment did NOT change tenure — this is a commonly assumed but factually incorrect change.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1, 2, and 3 as correct but are uncertain about Statement 4, potentially accepting the tenure change as plausible given the scope of the 2019 amendment.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 4 first — the most likely trap: The 2019 amendment did not alter tenure. Tenure remains 3 years or age 70 — Statement 4 is incorrect.
Statements 1, 2, 3 are all verifiable 2019 amendment changes: mandatory woman member, up to five members, NCBC added as ex-officio.
Three statements are correct, one is incorrect — select option (b): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The tenure trap is classic temporal-swap misdirection. The 2019 amendment made several significant changes, and students who have a vague recollection of 'the 2019 amendment changed many things' often accept the tenure extension as one of them. In reality, tenure remained frozen at 3 years/70 years — an unchanged provision that UPSC uses to catch over-generalising students.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2019 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act introduced several specific changes to NHRC's structure. Candidates must distinguish between what changed and what remained constant.

Consider the following statements about changes introduced by the 2019 amendment:

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Mandatory woman member introduced | Correct |
| Maximum members raised to five | Correct |
| NCBC Chairperson added as ex-officio | Correct |
| Tenure extended to 5 years | Incorrect |

• Statement 4 is the critical trap: Tenure remains 3 years or until age 70, whichever is earlier — unchanged by 2019. NCPCR was also added alongside NCBC as an ex-officio member.

Value Addition:
• The original ex-officio list included: NCW, NCM, NCSC, NCST — the 2019 amendment added NCBC and NCPCR.
• Ex-officio members participate in NHRC proceedings but are distinct from full members in quorum calculations.
• No re-appointment is permitted after completion of term — ensures institutional independence.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC tenure, removal, and financial conditions
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly places the salary charge on Consolidated Fund but mismatches removal procedure with a Parliamentary address route, which applies to CAG and certain other officers but not NHRC members.
elimination_logic: Anchor Match: List I item A (Term of office) — 3 years or age 70 is unambiguous from the Act; matches List II item 2.
Anchor Match: List I item D (Salary and conditions) — charged to Consolidated Fund of India matches List II item 4; this signals financial autonomy.
Elimination: Removal of NHRC members follows the Supreme Court inquiry route (similar to SC judge removal), not a Parliamentary address — eliminate any option pairing C with 'Parliamentary address'.
The correct matching is A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4 — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the removal procedure of NHRC members with that of the CAG or Supreme Court judges removed via Parliamentary address. NHRC members are removed by the President only after a Supreme Court inquiry — not by Parliamentary address. Students who recall 'independent statutory body' and 'parliamentary accountability' conflate removal mechanisms.
solution.final_explanation:
Service conditions for NHRC Chairperson and members are governed by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, and reflect a design aimed at institutional independence.

Correct matches: A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4.

• A (Term of office) → 2 (3 years or until age 70): The tenure is the shorter of these two — not 5 years as sometimes assumed.
• B (Re-appointment after term) → 3 (Not eligible for re-appointment): This single-term restriction ensures members act without fear or favour.
• C (Removal procedure) → 1 (Presidential order after Supreme Court inquiry): The process mirrors removal of a Supreme Court judge, signalling the gravity of removal. It is NOT by Parliamentary address.
• D (Salary and conditions) → 4 (Charged to Consolidated Fund of India): This provision, mirroring constitutional offices, insulates NHRC from annual budget pressure.

Value Addition:
• 'Charged' expenditure means it is non-votable — Parliament cannot withhold it.
• The removal procedure via SC inquiry is shared with bodies like the Lokpal — not all statutory bodies enjoy this protection.
• Compare: SHRC members are also non-re-appointable, and their salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the State.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC one-year limitation on complaint admissibility
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who know both facts are correct but assume the limitation period exists because NHRC is 'like a court' — the actual reason is a specific statutory restriction that cannot be condoned even by the Commission, unlike courts.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. NHRC cannot admit a complaint filed more than one year after the alleged violation; this is a strict limitation under the Protection of Human Rights Act.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. NHRC does NOT have the power to condone delay for complaints beyond one year; this is precisely what distinguishes NHRC from civil courts, which can condone delay under the Limitation Act. R incorrectly states NHRC has condonation power.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer is (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: correct_option is 'c' — matches the final elimination step.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap adds 'in exceptional circumstances' condonation power to NHRC that it does not actually possess. Courts under the Limitation Act can condone delay for sufficient cause. NHRC cannot — the one-year bar is absolute under Section 36(2) of the PHR Act. Students who assimilate NHRC with judicial bodies assume it also has inherent condonation discretion.
solution.final_explanation:
The one-year limitation rule is a critical and frequently tested jurisdictional restriction on NHRC's admissibility of complaints.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Section 36(2) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 explicitly bars NHRC from inquiring into a complaint filed more than one year after the date of the alleged violation. This is a hard statutory ceiling.
• Reason (R) — Incorrect: NHRC does NOT have the power to condone delay beyond one year 'in exceptional circumstances.' This is a false attribution. Unlike courts operating under the Limitation Act, NHRC cannot extend this period for any reason, no matter how compelling. This is precisely what makes the one-year rule a jurisdiction-limiting provision, not merely a procedural guideline.
• Causal relationship: Since R itself is factually wrong, it cannot explain A. Option (c) is correct.

Value Addition:
• Courts (civil and criminal) can condone delay for sufficient cause under Sections 5 and 14 of the Limitation Act — NHRC enjoys no such discretion.
• By contrast, NHRC can act suo motu even without a complaint — the limitation period applies only to complaints filed by petitioners.
• The strict limitation encourages timely reporting of custodial deaths and encounter killings, for which 24-hour reporting norms exist.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) places the NHRC's Section 19 armed forces restriction as coming after the 2006 amendment, when in fact it was part of the original 1993 Act — students who think restrictions were added later fall for this.
elimination_logic: Anchor: Protection of Human Rights Act enacted in 1993 — this is the starting point and must come first in any sequence.

The 2006 amendment came before the 2019 amendment — any option reversing this order is eliminated.
Correct order: PHR Act 1993 → Section 19 limitation (original, 1993) → 2006 Amendment → 2019 Amendment expanding membership and eligibility — option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 and its subsequent amendments trace NHRC's jurisdictional and compositional evolution.

Correct chronological order: Original PHR Act 1993 (including Section 19 armed forces restriction) → First amendment in 2006 → Second amendment in 2019.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Places armed forces restriction after 2006, which is wrong — it was part of the original 1993 legislation.
• Option (b) — Correct: Section 19's restriction on NHRC's authority over armed forces complaints is original to the 1993 Act. The 2006 amendment preceded the 2019 amendment.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Reverses the 2006 and 2019 amendments.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Incorrectly sequences all elements.

Value Addition:
• Section 19 of the PHR Act, 1993 is among the most criticised provisions — it restricts NHRC from directly investigating armed forces.
• The 2019 amendment is the most substantive, expanding chairperson eligibility, membership ceiling, mandatory woman member, and ex-officio members.
• The 2006 amendment primarily dealt with procedural aspects and SHRC provisions.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 19 armed forces restriction and NHRC-SHRC jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) suggesting NHRC can conduct a direct inquiry because the complaint relates to civilians is the strongest distractor; students who know Section 19 blocks armed forces complaints but assume 'civilian victim = NHRC jurisdiction' fall for this, missing that the restriction attaches to the agency complained against, not the victim's identity.
elimination_logic: Identify the complaint's target: A paramilitary force — this triggers Section 19 analysis.
Section 19 restricts NHRC from direct inquiry into armed forces complaints; however, paramilitary forces in civilian areas create a 'grey zone' — NHRC can seek a report from the Central Government.
NHRC cannot transfer to SHRC because the complaint involves a Central Government paramilitary force — SHRC cannot investigate Central Government employees.
NHRC's correct course of action: Seek a report from the Central Government under Section 19 and make recommendations based on it — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap assumes 'armed forces exception' applies only to the Army, Navy, and Air Force. Section 19 covers all armed forces of the Union. Paramilitary forces (CRPF, BSF) deployed by the Central Government fall within this grey zone — NHRC cannot directly inquire but must route its engagement through the Central Government, a nuance most students miss.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 19 of the Protection of Human Rights Act creates a unique jurisdictional constraint: NHRC cannot conduct a direct inquiry against 'armed forces.' The Act defines armed forces broadly to include paramilitary forces of the Union deployed in internal security roles.

Scenario analysis: A CRPF unit (Central paramilitary) is accused of excess use of force against civilians in a conflict-affected state.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: NHRC cannot transfer such a complaint to the SHRC — SHRC has no jurisdiction over Central Government forces.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: NHRC cannot conduct a direct inquiry even when the victims are civilians. The restriction attaches to the agency complained against, not the complainant's identity.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Closing the complaint outright is not mandated — NHRC retains a limited role.
• Option (d) — Correct: Under Section 19, NHRC can seek a report from the Central Government on the incident and, based on that report, make recommendations. It cannot investigate directly but is not entirely powerless.

Value Addition:
• This grey zone between paramilitary forces and the civilian administration is one of the most criticised aspects of the PHR Act.
• NHRC issued landmark guidelines in 1997 on encounter killings, requiring mandatory magisterial inquiry and reporting to NHRC.
• State police forces (unlike paramilitary) are NOT covered by Section 19 — NHRC can directly investigate complaints against state police.

concepts_used: Remedial Powers and Recommendations of NHRC
Structural Criticisms and Independence Concerns

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC recommendatory vs. binding powers
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'approach Supreme Court for directions on behalf of a victim' sounds like an enforcement power; students confuse NHRC approaching a court (which is real) with NHRC directly enforcing its recommendations (which is not permitted).
elimination_logic: Identify which options are genuine powers of NHRC: recommending compensation, recommending prosecution, approaching SC/HC — all are real powers.

Option (a) — 'Issue binding directions to State Governments to pay compensation within a fixed time': NHRC can only recommend, not issue binding directions. Government must comply or explain — this is a fabricated power.
Options (b), (c), (d) are all genuine NHRC powers confirmed by the PHR Act.
The odd-one-out is option (a) — a plausible-fabrication of enforcement authority NHRC does not possess.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap creates an option that sounds like the logical extension of NHRC's role. Since NHRC can recommend compensation, students assume it can also 'order' or 'direct' payment — blurring the quasi-judicial/judicial line. Only courts can issue binding directions; NHRC can only recommend and, if ignored, approach a court.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's remedial powers are carefully circumscribed by the Protection of Human Rights Act — it is a recommendatory body, not a binding judicial authority.

• Option (a) — Does NOT belong: NHRC cannot issue binding directions to State Governments. Its recommendations are non-binding; the government must comply or explain. This is the defining structural limitation of NHRC.
• Option (b) — Genuine power: NHRC can recommend payment of compensation to victims of human rights violations.
• Option (c) — Genuine power: NHRC can approach the Supreme Court or High Courts for appropriate directions when its recommendations are ignored — an indirect enforcement mechanism.
• Option (d) — Genuine power: NHRC can recommend initiation of proceedings for prosecution against responsible officials.

Value Addition:
• The 'toothless tiger' criticism of NHRC stems precisely from this non-binding character of its recommendations.
• NHRC can also recommend amendment of laws or rules as a systemic remedy — not just individual compensation.
• Compare: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has more binding interim powers than NHRC.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC-SHRC jurisdictional division and exclusivity

statement_analysis.statement: The NHRC can take up complaints against State Government employees even if a State Human Rights Commission is already inquiring into the same matter.
statement_analysis.reason: The PHR Act prohibits NHRC from investigating matters already pending before SHRCs or other commissions — this avoids jurisdictional overlap and double inquiry.

statement_analysis.statement: A State Human Rights Commission cannot investigate complaints against officers and personnel of the Central Government.
statement_analysis.reason: SHRC's jurisdiction is confined to state-level matters. Central Government employees are within the exclusive domain of NHRC — SHRCs have no authority over them.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who know NHRC has wide jurisdiction and assume 'concurrent jurisdiction' means NHRC can always act alongside SHRC; the Act specifically prohibits this duplication.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NHRC explicitly cannot investigate matters pending before SHRCs — Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: SHRC cannot touch Central Government employees — this is exclusive NHRC territory — Statement 2 is correct.
With Statement 1 incorrect and Statement 2 correct, select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 implies NHRC has overriding concurrent jurisdiction — 'even if SHRC is already inquiring.' The PHR Act prevents this to avoid jurisdictional duplication. Students who associate NHRC with higher authority assume it can always override or run parallel to SHRC.
solution.final_explanation:
The division of jurisdiction between NHRC and SHRCs is carefully demarcated under the PHR Act to prevent institutional overlap and ensure efficient redress.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: NHRC cannot take up a matter already pending before an SHRC or any other commission. The Act explicitly prohibits parallel inquiry to avoid inconsistent findings and institutional confusion.
• Statement 2 — Correct: SHRCs are restricted to state-level matters. They have no authority over Central Government employees, armed forces personnel, or Central paramilitary forces. These complaints belong exclusively to NHRC.

Value Addition:
• If a state has not constituted an SHRC, NHRC fills the gap and assumes jurisdiction for that state's complaints.
• NHRC can transfer a complaint to the appropriate SHRC if the matter relates exclusively to state government functioning.
• Both NHRC and SHRCs lack direct enforcement power — both are recommendatory bodies sharing this structural limitation.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC civil court powers during inquiry
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Code of Criminal Procedure' is the strongest distractor because NHRC deals with criminal acts like custodial deaths and encounter killings, leading students to assume its inquiry powers derive from CrPC rather than CPC.
elimination_logic: NHRC is a quasi-judicial body conducting inquiry, not a criminal court — CrPC governs criminal prosecutions, not inquiries by commissions.
The PHR Act explicitly grants NHRC the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure — this matches the investigative (not punitive) nature of its proceedings.
Eliminate CrPC (criminal), Evidence Act (evidentiary standards in courts), and Contempt of Courts Act (judicial contempt) as options.
The blank is correctly filled with 'Code of Civil Procedure' — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes 'Code of Civil Procedure' with 'Code of Criminal Procedure.' NHRC handles complaints about criminal acts but is not a criminal court. Its inquiry powers are structured on civil court powers — summons, evidence, document requisition — all characteristic of CPC, not CrPC.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's inquiry powers are specifically calibrated to enable effective investigation without conferring criminal trial authority.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Evidence Act governs admissibility in courts; NHRC's powers are not described in reference to this Act.
• Option (b) — Correct: The PHR Act grants NHRC all the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure for the purpose of inquiry — including summoning witnesses, compelling document production, and receiving affidavit evidence.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: CrPC governs criminal procedure and trial; NHRC is not a criminal court and cannot use CrPC powers.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Contempt of Courts Act applies to courts; NHRC is not a court of record.

Value Addition:
• NHRC can utilize investigation agencies of Central or State Governments during inquiry — a significant power multiplier.
• Civil court powers include: summoning and enforcing attendance, receiving evidence on affidavit, requisitioning public records.
• Despite these powers, NHRC cannot impose punishment — it can only recommend action to the government.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC annual report accountability vs. CAG-PAC mechanism
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) pairs NHRC reports with a 'Joint Parliamentary Committee on Human Rights' that does not exist, and sounds authoritative enough that students with a general sense of parliamentary oversight accept it as plausible.
elimination_logic: NHRC submits annual reports to Central/State Governments; these are laid before Parliament/Legislature — confirmed.
There is no parliamentary committee equivalent to PAC that scrutinises NHRC recommendations — eliminate options claiming such a committee exists.
CAG reports are examined by PAC — this is an established fact and a genuine pairing.
The correctly matched pair is: NHRC annual report is laid before Parliament with a memorandum of action taken (not examined by a dedicated scrutiny committee) — option (d) correctly captures this.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges NHRC's accountability mechanism with CAG's mechanism. Since CAG has a PAC to scrutinise its reports, students assume NHRC must have an equivalent. No such committee exists — NHRC reports are laid before Parliament, but no dedicated scrutiny mechanism follows, which is a recognised governance gap.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's accountability mechanism is weaker than that of many other statutory bodies because no dedicated parliamentary committee scrutinises its recommendations.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: NHRC does not submit its report directly to the Supreme Court; it submits to the Central Government and concerned State Governments.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: No 'Joint Parliamentary Committee on Human Rights' exists in India's parliamentary structure — this is a fabricated entity.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: NHRC reports are not examined by the Public Accounts Committee; PAC scrutinises CAG reports on public expenditure, not human rights recommendations.
• Option (d) — Correct: NHRC's annual report is submitted to the Central Government and laid before Parliament along with a memorandum indicating what action has been taken on its recommendations — this is the actual accountability mechanism.

Value Addition:
• Compare: CAG reports → examined by PAC; NHRC reports → laid before Parliament with action-taken memorandum but no equivalent scrutiny body.
• This absence of a dedicated scrutiny committee is cited as a democratic accountability gap in NHRC's design.
• State-level NHRC equivalent reports go to respective State Legislatures.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC Paris Principles and GANHRI A-status

statement_analysis.statement: The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 incorporates rights guaranteed under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) through its definition of 'human rights.'
statement_analysis.reason: The Act defines 'human rights' as rights relating to life, liberty, equality, and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants — specifically referencing ICCPR and ICESCR.

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC's 'A-status' from the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) means its resolutions are legally binding on the Indian Government under international law.
statement_analysis.reason: GANHRI's 'A-status' accreditation enhances NHRC's international standing and allows it to engage with UN human rights mechanisms, but it does not make NHRC's resolutions legally binding under international law. The accreditation is a recognition of compliance with Paris Principles, not a source of binding authority.

statement_analysis.statement: The Paris Principles (1991) require national human rights institutions to be independent from the government, have a broad mandate, and be accessible to the public.
statement_analysis.reason: Paris Principles set the minimum standards for national human rights institutions: independence, broad human rights mandate, adequate resources, and public accessibility — all of which NHRC is evaluated against for its A-status.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) including Statement 2 as correct is the strongest distractor because 'A-status' sounds like a legal recognition that implies binding authority, and students unfamiliar with GANHRI's advisory role may accept this claim.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: PHR Act's definition of human rights explicitly incorporates ICCPR and ICESCR — correct.
Reject Statement 2: GANHRI A-status is an accreditation for UN engagement, not a source of binding legal obligation on the Indian Government — incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Paris Principles' requirements of independence, broad mandate, and public accessibility are the evaluative standards for A-status — correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses 'A-status' and 'legally binding under international law' in combination — a partial-truth trap. A-status is real and significant (enabling NHRC to participate in UN forums), but it confers no binding legal obligation on India. Students impressed by 'A-status' as a marker of credibility assume it implies legal enforcement power.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's international dimension is shaped by the Paris Principles and its GANHRI accreditation, but students must be precise about what these confer.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The definitional inclusivity of ICCPR and ICESCR in the PHR Act is a key feature — it means NHRC can address violations of internationally recognized civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights under domestic law.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: GANHRI's A-status enhances NHRC's ability to participate in UN Human Rights Council proceedings and advisory mechanisms. It does not create binding obligations for the Indian Government — NHRC's recommendations remain non-binding domestically and internationally.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Paris Principles (1991) require: independence from government, pluralism in composition, broad mandate covering all human rights, adequate funding, and accessibility to all members of the public.

Value Addition:
• NHRC represents India at GANHRI and at UN human rights forums — a diplomatic function beyond domestic adjudication.
• India ratified ICCPR and ICESCR in 1979, predating the PHR Act by over a decade.
• 'B-status' institutions have limited UN engagement — only A-status bodies can fully participate in Human Rights Council sessions.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC complaint admissibility conditions

statement_analysis.statement: Complaints before the NHRC must be filed only in English or Hindi — regional language petitions are not entertained.
statement_analysis.reason: NHRC accepts complaints in any language recognized under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, reflecting its accessibility mandate under the Paris Principles.

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC rejects all anonymous complaints categorically, similar to the practice under the Right to Information Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike the RTI framework where anonymous complaints are outright rejected, NHRC's treatment of anonymous complaints is discretionary — it may or may not act on them based on the seriousness of the allegation.

statement_analysis.statement: The NHRC cannot examine a complaint if the complainant has an alternative remedy that is currently being pursued before a competent court or authority.
statement_analysis.reason: NHRC follows judicial restraint principles and declines to investigate matters where the complainant is pursuing an alternative remedy before a court or other body — avoiding duplication of proceedings.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) stating Statement 2 alone is incorrect tempts students who know NHRC accepts regional languages but are uncertain about the anonymous complaint distinction, potentially thinking the RTI parallel is valid.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NHRC accepts petitions in any Eighth Schedule language — Statement 1 is incorrect (which satisfies the 'NOT correct' question).
Evaluate Statement 2: NHRC's approach to anonymous complaints is discretionary, not the outright rejection practiced under RTI — Statement 2 is also incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The alternative remedy restriction is a genuine admissibility condition — Statement 3 is correct.
Both Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — select option (c): 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a comparison with RTI. Under RTI, anonymous complaints are rejected. Under NHRC's framework, anonymous complaints may be acted upon at the Commission's discretion — a meaningful distinction that students who apply RTI rules to NHRC will miss. The scope-extension trap makes the RTI rule appear universal.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's complaint admissibility conditions balance accessibility with judicial restraint principles.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (satisfies 'NOT correct'): NHRC accepts complaints in any language listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution — not just English or Hindi. This is a direct application of the Paris Principles' public accessibility requirement.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (satisfies 'NOT correct'): NHRC is not bound to reject anonymous complaints. Unlike RTI (where anonymous petitions are inadmissible), NHRC exercises discretion — particularly when the allegation is serious, like a custodial death reported anonymously.
• Statement 3 — Correct: NHRC will not investigate if the complainant is simultaneously pursuing the matter before a court or another competent body — this prevents parallel proceedings.

Value Addition:
• There are currently 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule — complaints in any of these are valid for NHRC.
• RTI Act, 2005 requires the applicant's name and address — NHRC has no such mandatory requirement.
• NHRC can also act suo motu — meaning it does not always need a formal complaint to begin inquiry.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC custodial death reporting norms and encounter guidelines

statement_analysis.statement: State governments are required to report all custodial deaths to the NHRC within 24 hours of occurrence.
statement_analysis.reason: NHRC's guidelines mandate that state governments report custodial deaths (and rape) to the NHRC within 24 hours — failure to report itself constitutes a violation that NHRC can take suo motu cognizance of.

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC issued guidelines on encounter killings in 1997, requiring a mandatory magisterial inquiry and submission of a report to the NHRC.
statement_analysis.reason: NHRC's 1997 guidelines on encounter killings established that every encounter killing must be followed by a magisterial inquiry, and the report must be submitted to the NHRC — a critical accountability measure.

statement_analysis.statement: Non-reporting of a custodial death by a state government to the NHRC does not itself constitute a human rights violation — only the underlying custodial death does.
statement_analysis.reason: Non-reporting is itself treated as a violation — NHRC can take suo motu cognizance based on non-reporting alone, making the reporting obligation substantive and not merely procedural.

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC's jurisdiction over encounter killings by paramilitary forces is identical to its jurisdiction over encounter killings by state police forces.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 19 creates a jurisdictional distinction — NHRC can directly inquire into state police encounters but only seek a report from the Central Government for paramilitary encounters. The jurisdictions are not identical.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is the strongest distractor for students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 2 as true and correctly reject Statement 3, but then mistakenly accept Statement 4 as true because they overlook the Section 19 paramilitary distinction.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: 24-hour custodial death reporting norm is well-established NHRC guideline — correct.
Confirm Statement 2: 1997 encounter killing guidelines requiring magisterial inquiry and NHRC report — correct.
Reject Statement 3: Non-reporting is itself a violation; NHRC can take suo motu cognizance — Statement 3 is incorrect.

Reject Statement 4: Section 19 creates a distinction between state police (direct inquiry) and paramilitary (report-based only) — jurisdictions are not identical — Statement 4 is incorrect. Only two statements (1 and 2) are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is a scope-extension trap that implies uniform NHRC jurisdiction across all security forces. The Section 19 distinction — state police vs. paramilitary — is the critical nuance. Students who have memorised 'NHRC investigates encounter killings' without distinguishing force types will accept Statement 4 as true.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's role in custodial deaths and encounter killings is one of its most significant and tested mandates.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 24-hour custodial death reporting | Correct |
| 1997 encounter killing guidelines | Correct |
| Non-reporting is not itself a violation | Incorrect |
| NHRC's jurisdiction is identical for state police and paramilitary | Incorrect |

• Statements 3 and 4 are incorrect: Non-reporting is independently actionable by NHRC. Paramilitary encounters fall under Section 19 — NHRC can only seek a report from the Central Government, not conduct a direct inquiry, unlike state police encounters.

Value Addition:
• NHRC took suo motu cognizance of post-Godhra riots (2002) and Manipur encounter cases — landmark uses of this power.
• The 24-hour reporting rule for custodial deaths and rape is among NHRC's most impactful operational guidelines.
• COVID-19 migrant crisis was another instance of NHRC's suo motu engagement — expanding the scope of 'human rights' to socioeconomic emergencies.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC prison inspection with prior notice vs. SC inherent power
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who know both facts are correct and assume the prior notice requirement 'explains' NHRC's non-binding status — a causal link that does not exist; the prior notice requirement and non-binding status are independent features.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. NHRC or its representatives can visit jails and detention institutions to study living conditions, but prior notice to the State Government is required.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. NHRC's recommendations following inspections are non-binding — the government must comply or explain but is not legally compelled.

Step 3: Does R causally or logically explain A? — No. The requirement of prior notice before inspection is not caused by or related to the non-binding nature of NHRC's recommendations. Prior notice is a procedural design choice; non-binding recommendations are a substantive limitation. These are independent features of NHRC's framework.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → option (b). Confirm: correct_option is 'b'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap implies that NHRC requires prior notice for inspections because its recommendations are non-binding — suggesting a causal connection that does not exist. Prior notice is a procedural requirement reflecting cooperative federalism; non-binding recommendations are a substantive design choice. Students who see both as 'limitations' conflate them causally.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's prison inspection powers and the non-binding nature of its recommendations are two independent but related features of its operational framework.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: NHRC can depute its representatives to visit prisons and detention facilities to assess living conditions and report violations. However, unlike the Supreme Court, which can conduct surprise inspections, NHRC must give prior notice to the State Government.
• Reason (R) — Correct: NHRC's findings from such inspections result in recommendations — not binding orders. The State Government must either comply or provide an explanation, but cannot be directly penalised for non-compliance.
• Causal relationship: R does not explain A. Prior notice is required not because recommendations are non-binding, but because NHRC operates within a framework of cooperative engagement with state governments. The two features are structurally independent.

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court has inherent supervisory jurisdiction over prisons and can issue binding directions without prior notice — a stark contrast with NHRC.
• Prior notice is seen as both a safeguard (for state sovereignty) and a limitation (allowing states to prepare).
• NHRC's prison reports have contributed to national discourse on prison reforms, including recommendations on overcrowding and undertrial detention.

concepts_used: Distinction Between NHRC and Human Rights Courts

solution.concept_anchor: Human Rights Courts under PHR Act — Sessions Court designation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) conflates Human Rights Courts with NHRC's own benches or extensions, leading students to think NHRC itself establishes regional hearing centres rather than the Act mandating separate district-level courts.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): NHRC does not establish its own regional benches called Human Rights Courts — these are separate courts at the district level under the Sessions Court system.
Eliminate (b): Human Rights Courts are not Family Courts — they are designated Sessions Courts, which have criminal trial jurisdiction.
Confirm (c): The PHR Act mandates that each district may have a Human Rights Court, which is a designated Sessions Court — with a Special Public Prosecutor appointed by the State Government.
Eliminate (d): Civil courts do not exercise Human Rights Court jurisdiction — these are criminal courts (Sessions Courts) with specific jurisdiction over human rights offences.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges NHRC (quasi-judicial, recommendatory) with Human Rights Courts (criminal trial jurisdiction at district level). Students aware of NHRC's jurisdiction assume 'human rights courts' are NHRC sub-units. In fact, they are entirely separate institutions — Sessions Courts designated under the PHR Act — with different powers and a different operational chain.
solution.final_explanation:
The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 mandates a two-tier institutional structure: NHRC at the national level (quasi-judicial) and Human Rights Courts at the district level (judicial, with criminal trial powers).

• Option (a) — Incorrect: NHRC does not establish regional branches called Human Rights Courts. They are separate district-level courts.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Human Rights Courts are not Family Courts. Family Courts handle matrimonial and custody matters under a different statute.
• Option (c) — Correct: Human Rights Courts are designated Sessions Courts at the district level, with a Special Public Prosecutor appointed by the State Government for each such court.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Sessions Court (criminal court) is designated — not a civil court. Human rights offences require criminal trial jurisdiction.

Value Addition:
• Human Rights Courts are grossly underutilised — most states have not operationalized them, making them a governance failure on paper.
• The Special Public Prosecutor appointment by the State Government mirrors the Designated Court mechanism under other special legislation.
• NHRC's quasi-judicial recommendations and Human Rights Courts' binding criminal judgments represent complementary but distinct accountability tracks.

solution.concept_anchor: 2019 amendment: what changed vs. what did not change

statement_analysis.statement: The 2019 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act expanded the eligibility for the post of NHRC Chairperson to include retired Judges of the Supreme Court in addition to the retired Chief Justice of India.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the most significant compositional change of the 2019 amendment — expanding Chairperson eligibility from 'only retired CJI' to 'retired CJI or any retired Judge of the Supreme Court.'

statement_analysis.statement: The 2019 amendment changed the tenure of the NHRC Chairperson and members from three years to five years to align with international human rights institution norms.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2019 amendment did not alter tenure. It remains 3 years or until age 70, whichever is earlier. This 'tenure extension' claim is a common misconception and a deliberate UPSC trap.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairpersons of both the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) were added as ex-officio members of the NHRC by the 2019 amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2019 amendment added NCPCR and NCBC Chairpersons to the ex-officio membership list, supplementing the original members: NCW, NCM, NCSC, and NCST Chairpersons.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) including Statement 2 alongside Statements 1 and 3 is the strongest distractor — students who correctly identify 1 and 3 as true but are misled by the plausible-sounding 'international alignment' rationale for a tenure change will pick this.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Chairperson eligibility expansion from 'retired CJI only' to 'retired CJI or retired SC Judge' is the hallmark change of the 2019 amendment — correct.
Reject Statement 2: Tenure remains 3 years/70 years; no international alignment rationale was cited in the amendment; this is a fabricated claim — incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Both NCPCR and NCBC Chairpersons were added as ex-officio members — correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses 'international human rights institution norms' as a justification for a tenure change that never happened. This is a temporal-swap combined with plausible-fabrication — adding an authoritative-sounding rationale to a false claim about an amendment. Students who are uncertain about the exact tenure provisions often accept the 'alignment' rationale as credible.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2019 amendment made targeted changes to NHRC's composition — not to tenure or removal. Precision on what changed and what did not is essential.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Chairperson eligibility expansion is the most tested change. Before 2019, only a retired CJI could head NHRC. Post-2019, any retired Supreme Court judge qualifies.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Tenure is unchanged at 3 years or age 70. The claim about 'international alignment' is entirely fabricated — no such rationale appears in the amendment or its Statement of Objects and Reasons.
• Statement 3 — Correct: NCPCR and NCBC were added to the ex-officio membership. The original six ex-officio members (NCW, NCM, NCSC, NCST, and two others) expanded to eight with these additions.

Value Addition:
• The 2019 amendment also made it mandatory to have at least one woman member — a distinct change from the ex-officio expansion.
• Ex-officio members participate in NHRC proceedings relating to their respective commissions' mandates.
• The tenure rule of 3 years/70 years applies equally to the Chairperson and all members — there is no differential tenure within the Commission.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC structural independence limitations

statement_analysis.statement: The NHRC is structurally dependent on the government for investigative staff and agencies, which critics argue compromises its functional independence.
statement_analysis.reason: The PHR Act allows NHRC to utilise services of Central or State Government investigation agencies — it has no independent police or investigative arm, creating a structural dependence that is widely acknowledged as limiting its effectiveness.

statement_analysis.statement: Since the High-Powered Committee for NHRC appointments is chaired by the Prime Minister and includes the Home Minister, the NHRC's appointment process is completely immune from executive influence due to the mandatory inclusion of opposition leaders.
statement_analysis.reason: The inclusion of opposition leaders mitigates but does not eliminate executive influence — the committee is still dominated by ruling party representatives (PM, Speaker, Home Minister), and 'completely immune' is an overstatement that does not reflect the structural reality or scholarly criticism.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) would mean both statements are correct, tempting students who agree with Statement 1 and read 'opposition leaders included' in Statement 2 as sufficient to make it fully accurate, missing the 'completely immune' overstatement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NHRC relies on government investigation agencies — no independent investigative arm exists. This structural dependence is a documented criticism — Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The phrase 'completely immune from executive influence' is factually indefensible. The PM, Speaker, and Home Minister all represent the ruling establishment. Bipartisan inclusion reduces, but cannot eliminate, executive influence — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a partial-truth: opposition leaders are indeed included, which is factually accurate. But the conclusion drawn — 'completely immune from executive influence' — is an overstatement that makes the statement false. Students who focus on the factual premise (opposition leaders included) miss the false conclusion (complete immunity).
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's structural independence is constrained in two important ways: investigative dependence and appointment vulnerability.

• Statement 1 — Correct: NHRC lacks an independent investigation wing. It borrows officers and agencies from Central and State Governments. This means the very bodies it may be investigating can potentially influence the investigation process — a structurally acknowledged limitation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: While the High-Powered Committee does include Leaders of Opposition from both Houses (ensuring some bipartisan oversight), it is chaired by the Prime Minister and includes the Home Minister and Speaker — all from the ruling establishment. 'Completely immune' is a false absolute. The bipartisan structure reduces, not eliminates, executive influence. This is a well-documented structural criticism of NHRC.

Value Addition:
• The 'toothless tiger' critique of NHRC rests on three pillars: non-binding recommendations, investigative dependence, and appointment process vulnerabilities.
• Compare the CBI Director appointment committee — it includes the CJI — providing judicial insulation absent from the NHRC process.
• Paris Principles require genuine independence — critics argue India's NHRC falls short of this standard in appointment and operations.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC interim relief and SC/HC approach power
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) 'National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission' sounds appropriate because NCDRC is also a quasi-judicial body that grants interim relief, leading students to compare NHRC unfavourably with it — but the correct contrast is with purely advisory bodies like NCPRI.
elimination_logic: The blank refers to a body that distinguishes NHRC from purely advisory institutions — NHRC's interim relief power is the distinguishing feature.
NHRC can grant interim relief during inquiry AND approach SC/HC for stay orders — this is more than purely advisory bodies possess.
The comparison is with advisory bodies like the National Campaign for People's Right to Information (NCPRI) — which has no interim relief power.
The correct answer is 'approach the Supreme Court or High Courts for stay orders or directions on behalf of the victim' — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap creates option (b) — 'order immediate release of a detained person' — which sounds like a natural human rights power but exceeds NHRC's statutory authority. Only courts can order release; NHRC can only approach courts to seek such directions on behalf of victims.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's interim relief powers distinguish it from purely advisory bodies but fall short of judicial enforcement authority.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The NCDRC (National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission) is a separate quasi-judicial body. NHRC is not comparable with NCDRC in this context; the contrast intended is with advisory bodies lacking any interim power.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: NHRC cannot directly order the immediate release of a detained person — only courts can do so through habeas corpus or bail orders. NHRC can approach courts to seek such directions.
• Option (c) — Correct: NHRC's interim relief power includes the ability to approach the Supreme Court or High Courts for stay orders or appropriate directions on behalf of the victim during the pendency of its inquiry. This is what distinguishes NHRC from purely advisory bodies.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: NHRC cannot impose fines on state officials — it lacks punitive powers; fines are judicial instruments.

Value Addition:
• NHRC's power to approach SC/HC is a significant enforcement-adjacent tool — it converts NHRC's quasi-judicial role into a conduit for binding court orders.
• Compare: National Commission for Right to Information (NCPRI) is a civil society body with no legal powers; NHRC at least has interim relief and court-approach powers.
• Interim relief does not wait for final inquiry — it can be granted during the pendency of proceedings.

(b) Order the immediate release of any person found to be illegally detained by a State authority
(c) Approach the Supreme Court or a High Court for stay orders or other appropriate directions on behalf of the victim
(d) Impose monetary fines on state officials responsible for the violation pending completion of the inquiry

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC role during disasters vs. NDMA enforcement architecture

statement_analysis.statement: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and the NHRC share the same enforcement architecture — both can issue binding directions to State Governments in the event of a disaster or mass atrocity.
statement_analysis.reason: NDMA has statutory power to issue binding directions to State Governments and their agencies under the Disaster Management Act, 2005. NHRC can only recommend — it cannot issue binding directions. Their enforcement architectures are fundamentally different.

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC took suo motu cognizance of the COVID-19 migrant crisis, demonstrating that 'human rights' under the PHR Act can extend to socioeconomic distress situations.
statement_analysis.reason: NHRC's suo motu cognizance during the 2020 COVID-19 migrant crisis is a documented instance of the Commission interpreting 'human rights' (including dignity and livelihood) broadly enough to cover acute socioeconomic distress.

statement_analysis.statement: When a state government fails to act on NHRC recommendations following a mass atrocity, the NHRC can directly penalise state officials through fines or suspension orders.
statement_analysis.reason: NHRC has no power to directly penalise state officials. It can approach the Supreme Court or High Court for appropriate directions — but cannot itself impose fines or suspensions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) stating both Statements 1 and 3 are not correct is the strongest distractor; students unsure about NDMA's exact enforcement architecture may tentatively accept Statement 1 as partially true, making the 'both 1 and 3' combination seem uncertain.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NDMA has binding direction power under the Disaster Management Act; NHRC can only recommend — these are not the same enforcement architecture. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: NHRC's COVID-19 migrant crisis engagement is documented — Statement 2 is correct, so it does NOT satisfy the 'NOT correct' criterion.
Evaluate Statement 3: NHRC cannot directly penalise officials — only recommend or approach courts. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Statement 1 merges NHRC and NDMA as if they share enforcement powers because both respond to disasters. NDMA's binding direction power under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 is a fundamentally different statutory authority from NHRC's recommendatory mandate. Students who recall 'both deal with crises' conflate their legal powers.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's engagement during disasters and mass atrocities reveals both its activist potential and its structural limitations.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: NDMA and NHRC have entirely different enforcement architectures. NDMA (Disaster Management Act, 2005) can issue binding directions to state governments and their agencies. NHRC can only recommend — no binding directions, no coercive enforcement.
• Statement 2 — Correct: NHRC's suo motu intervention during the COVID-19 migrant crisis (2020) is a significant precedent. By seeking reports on migrant workers' conditions, NHRC interpreted 'dignity' and 'life' broadly to include socioeconomic rights during a crisis.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: NHRC cannot directly penalise state officials through fines or suspension orders. Its options on non-compliance are: approach SC/HC for directions, or publish the non-compliance in its annual report. Direct punitive power is absent.

Value Addition:
• NHRC's interventions in post-Godhra riots (2002), Manipur encounter cases, and COVID-19 migrant crisis are landmark suo motu actions.
• NDMA was established under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 — a post-tsunami legislative response.
• NHRC's lack of direct enforcement distinguishes it sharply from NDMA and judiciary in disaster response capability.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps the Chairperson eligibility criteria between NHRC and SHRC — students who confuse post-2019 NHRC criteria with SHRC criteria will be trapped here.
elimination_logic: Anchor: SHRC Chairperson = retired Chief Justice of a High Court — this is a fixed and well-known fact; matches A-3.
NHRC Chairperson post-2019 = retired CJI or any retired SC Judge — matches B-1.
NHRC appointment is by President; SHRC appointment is by Governor — matches C-4 (NHRC by President) and D-2 (SHRC by Governor).
Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exchanges NHRC and SHRC Chairperson eligibility criteria. A retired Chief Justice of a High Court heads SHRC; post-2019, a retired CJI or retired SC Judge heads NHRC. Students who have partially memorised one set apply it to both, creating the swap error. The appointment authority (President vs. Governor) adds a second layer of potential confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC and SHRC differ systematically in Chairperson eligibility, membership eligibility, and appointing authority.

Correct matches: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2.

• A (SHRC Chairperson eligibility) → 3 (Retired Chief Justice of a High Court): SHRC is headed by a retired HC Chief Justice — a lower court than NHRC's requirement.
• B (NHRC Chairperson eligibility post-2019) → 1 (Retired CJI or any retired Judge of the Supreme Court): Post-2019 expansion is the key change; pre-2019, only retired CJI was eligible.

Value Addition:
• SHRC's appointment committee includes the CM, Speaker of State Legislature, and Home Minister of the State — parallel structure to NHRC's national committee.
• Both Chairpersons have identical tenure: 3 years or age 70 — whichever is earlier.
• Neither Chairperson is eligible for re-appointment after completing their term.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC suo motu cognizance and one-year limitation rule
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) suggesting NHRC can take cognizance because the victim has no other remedy conflates the 'fill-in provision' (where no SHRC exists) with the one-year limitation rule, leading students to think lack of alternative remedy overrides the time bar.
elimination_logic: Identify the critical variable: the complaint is filed 18 months after the violation — beyond the one-year statutory bar.
NHRC cannot condone delay beyond one year — this is an absolute bar under Section 36(2), not subject to exceptions for any reason including absence of SHRC.
Eliminate (a): NHRC cannot transfer a time-barred complaint to SHRC — time bar applies regardless of transfer.
Eliminate (c): Absence of alternative remedy does not override the one-year bar.
Eliminate (d): Suo motu power does not override the one-year limitation for complaints filed by petitioners — the limitation applies to petitions, not to NHRC's own cognizance of fresh violations.
Correct answer (b): NHRC must decline to inquire into the complaint as it is filed beyond the one-year limitation period.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap adds qualifiers ('no SHRC exists,' 'no alternative remedy') that seem legally compelling but do not override the one-year absolute bar. Students who know the NHRC fill-in provision (assuming jurisdiction when no SHRC exists) misapply it to excuse the time bar. The one-year limitation is non-waivable regardless of surrounding circumstances.
solution.final_explanation:
The one-year limitation under Section 36(2) of the PHR Act is an absolute jurisdictional bar — not a procedural one that can be excused by equitable considerations.

Scenario analysis: A complaint is filed with NHRC 18 months after the alleged violation. No SHRC exists in the state. The complaint relates to a State Government official.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: NHRC cannot transfer a time-barred complaint to SHRC. The limitation is on NHRC's own jurisdiction; transfer does not revive an expired complaint.
• Option (b) — Correct: NHRC must decline to inquire. The 18-month delay exceeds the statutory one-year bar. Unlike courts that can condone delay for sufficient cause, NHRC has no such discretion — the bar is absolute.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Absence of SHRC allows NHRC to assume jurisdiction for that state's complaints, but this applies to timely complaints — it does not suspend the one-year limitation period.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: NHRC's suo motu cognizance applies when it independently discovers a violation — it cannot be used by a petitioner to backdoor a time-barred complaint by framing it as a suo motu trigger.

Value Addition:
• Suo motu cognizance is NHRC's own initiation — it is not triggered by a petitioner's request.
• The one-year bar is one of the most practically consequential limitations — victims of prolonged or concealed violations often find themselves barred.
• Courts (under Limitation Act) vs. NHRC (under PHR Act): the contrast in condonation power is a recurring UPSC comparative question.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC features that ensure independence vs. structural dependence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Removal only by Presidential order after SC inquiry' appears to be a limitation on independence because it involves the government, when in fact it is a protection of independence by requiring a rigorous judicial process before removal.
elimination_logic: Identify which three options genuinely protect NHRC's independence.
Option (a): Dependence on government investigation agencies is a structural dependence — it undermines, not ensures, independence. This is the odd-one-out.
Options (b), (c), (d) — non-re-appointment, removal via SC inquiry, and salary charged to Consolidated Fund — all protect independence.
The one that does NOT ensure independence is option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap places a genuine structural feature of NHRC (using government investigation agencies) alongside three independence-protecting features, making option (a) look like just another operational feature. Students who recall 'NHRC can use government agencies' as a power may not recognise it as a structural dependence that undermines independence.
solution.final_explanation:
Several features of NHRC's design are intended to ensure independence; one is a structural limitation that critics argue undermines it.

• Option (a) — The ODD ONE OUT: NHRC's dependence on Central or State Government investigation agencies is a structural weakness. Unlike independent institutions with their own investigative arms, NHRC must borrow from the very government whose agencies it may be investigating — a conflict of interest and independence concern.
• Option (b) — Protects independence: Non-eligibility for re-appointment means members have no incentive to appease the appointing authority for a future term.
• Option (c) — Protects independence: Removal only by Presidential order after a Supreme Court inquiry mirrors the protection given to Supreme Court judges — making arbitrary removal extremely difficult.
• Option (d) — Protects independence: Salary charged to the Consolidated Fund of India means Parliament cannot withhold funds to pressure the Commission.

Value Addition:
• The CBI also lacks a fully independent investigation wing — it is under the administrative control of the Department of Personnel and Training, creating a similar structural tension.
• Paris Principles require 'adequate resources' for national human rights institutions — financial dependence on government violates this in spirit.
• NHRC's independence is thus a matter of formal design (tenure, removal) but practical vulnerability (investigation and resources).

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC annual report vs. CAG-PAC scrutiny comparison
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who agree that both facts are true and instinctively assume 'no scrutiny committee = weaker democratic accountability' forms a causal chain explaining why reports are 'merely laid before Parliament' — but causation runs the other way: the absence of a scrutiny committee is the gap, not the explanation for why the report is laid before Parliament.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. NHRC annual reports are laid before Parliament along with a memorandum of action taken, but no dedicated scrutiny committee reviews them the way PAC reviews CAG reports.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. CAG reports are examined by the Public Accounts Committee, a standing committee of Parliament — this is a well-established fact.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — No. The reason NHRC reports lack a scrutiny committee is a design gap in the PHR Act — not because CAG has PAC. CAG's PAC mechanism is an independent feature of a different statutory framework; its existence does not causally explain why NHRC lacks an equivalent.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → option (b)... re-check: Both A and R are correct, R does not explain A → option (b). Confirm: correct_option is 'b'.
solution.final_explanation:
The comparison between NHRC's accountability mechanism and CAG's PAC-based scrutiny is a significant governance contrast, but the two facts are not causally linked.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: NHRC's annual report is submitted to the Central Government and laid before Parliament with an action-taken memorandum. Unlike CAG reports, there is no standing committee of Parliament that examines NHRC recommendations or holds the government accountable for non-compliance.
• Reason (R) — Correct: CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General) reports are indeed examined by the Public Accounts Committee — a well-established parliamentary oversight mechanism under Article 148 and parliamentary convention.
• Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The absence of a scrutiny committee for NHRC is a legislative design gap in the PHR Act — it is not caused by the existence of PAC for CAG. These are structurally independent features of different institutions. Option (b) is correct.

Value Addition:
• PAC examines CAG reports on public expenditure; Estimates Committee examines budget estimates — NHRC has neither equivalent.
• This democratic accountability gap is cited as a reason for NHRC's limited political impact despite significant findings.
• Some scholars argue Parliament should establish a Human Rights Oversight Committee similar to the Joint Committee on Human Rights in the UK Parliament.

solution.concept_anchor: NHRC jurisdictional scope and limitations

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC can take suo motu cognizance of human rights violations without waiting for a formal complaint to be filed.
statement_analysis.reason: The PHR Act explicitly empowers NHRC to initiate inquiry on its own motion — suo motu cognizance is a core power that distinguishes NHRC from purely complaint-driven bodies.

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC can investigate complaints against officers of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) deployed in a state, in the same manner as it investigates complaints against state police officers.
statement_analysis.reason: CRPF is a central paramilitary (armed force of the Union) — Section 19 prevents NHRC from directly investigating such complaints. NHRC can only seek a report from the Central Government, unlike its direct inquiry power over state police.

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC cannot take up a complaint that is already being investigated by a State Human Rights Commission in the same state.
statement_analysis.reason: The PHR Act explicitly prohibits NHRC from inquiring into a matter pending before an SHRC — this prevents jurisdictional overlap and duplicate proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: NHRC can investigate any human rights violation, including those committed more than one year ago, if the violation is of a continuing nature.
statement_analysis.reason: The one-year limitation under Section 36(2) is absolute — the PHR Act does not recognize a 'continuing violation' exception for extending this period, unlike some other limitation frameworks.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify 1 and 3 as true and correctly reject 2, but accept Statement 4 because 'continuing violation' doctrine exists in other legal frameworks (like international human rights law) and seems logically applicable to NHRC.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Suo motu power is explicitly granted — correct.
Reject Statement 2: CRPF is a paramilitary force of the Union; Section 19 prevents direct NHRC inquiry — incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: PHR Act prohibits NHRC from taking up matters pending before SHRCs — correct.
Reject Statement 4: PHR Act's one-year bar has no continuing violation exception unlike international law frameworks — incorrect.
Only two statements (1 and 3) are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 exploits familiarity with the 'continuing violation' doctrine common in international human rights law (ICCPR) and even some domestic judicial doctrines. Students who know NHRC interfaces with international law assume it has imported this exception. The PHR Act does not provide for it — the one-year bar remains absolute domestically.
solution.final_explanation:
NHRC's jurisdiction has clear inclusions and equally clear exclusions — precision on both is required.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Suo motu cognizance power | Correct |
| Same inquiry power over CRPF as state police | Incorrect |
| Cannot investigate matters pending before SHRC | Correct |
| Continuing violation exception to one-year bar | Incorrect |

• Statement 2 is incorrect: CRPF's central paramilitary status triggers Section 19 — NHRC must route engagement through the Central Government.
• Statement 4 is incorrect: 'Continuing violation' is an international human rights law concept not adopted in the PHR Act — the domestic one-year bar admits no exceptions.

Value Addition:
• State police forces are NOT covered by Section 19 — direct NHRC inquiry is possible against them.
• The 'continuing violation' doctrine allows international bodies like the Human Rights Committee (ICCPR) to consider older violations if they persist — India's domestic NHRC has no equivalent provision.
• NHRC's suo motu power has been used in cases of prison overcrowding, communal violence, and migrant distress — demonstrating its proactive institutional character.
